cues.text: An Augustinian Friar in Wittenberg
Martin Luther , born at Eisleben in 1483, entered the Augustinian order after a dramatic vow made during a thunderstorm and was ordained a priest in 1507.
By 1517 he was a professor of moral theology at the young University of Wittenberg, wrestling personally and academically with questions of sin, grace, and the assurance of salvation.
The Indulgence Controversy

That year, the Dominican friar Johann Tetzel was preaching an indulgence campaign nearby to raise funds officially designated for the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, promising remission of temporal punishment for sin in exchange for financial contributions.
Luther, troubled by what he saw as the crass commercialization and theological confusion surrounding these preached indulgences, drafted ninety-five propositions for academic debate.
The Posting at Wittenberg
According to long tradition, Luther nailed his Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences — the Ninety-Five Theses — to the Castle Church door at Wittenberg.
This was on October 31, 1517 , then the customary place for posting notices of academic disputations.
He also sent copies to Archbishop Albert of Mainz, whose diocese benefited from the indulgence sales, asking him to intervene.
Rapid Spread and Escalation

Though written for a local academic audience and largely in Latin, the theses were quickly translated, printed, and circulated across Germany, aided by the printing technology introduced barely sixty years earlier.

Rome responded by summoning Luther to explain himself; a 1518 debate at Augsburg with Cardinal Cajetan failed to produce a retraction, and the dispute widened over the following years into a fundamental challenge to papal authority itself.
Excommunication and the Diet of Worms
Pope Leo X formally condemned Luther's teachings in 1520 and excommunicated him the following year after Luther refused to recant.
Summoned before the Imperial Diet at Worms in 1521, Luther again declined to retract his positions.
He reportedly declared he could not act against conscience, a defiance that placed him under imperial ban even as sympathetic German princes shielded him from arrest.
Legacy

What began as a call for academic debate over indulgences rapidly became the opening act of the Protestant Reformation , permanently dividing Western Christendom into Catholic and Protestant traditions.
The controversy prompted the Catholic Church's own vigorous response at the Council of Trent decades later.
Meanwhile, Luther's own translation of the Bible into German and his doctrine of justification by faith alone reshaped Northern Europe's religious landscape for centuries to come.
